newsitem.title: USA: INTEL CLAIM SEEN LEADING TO SETTLEMENT.
newsitem.headline: INTEL CLAIM SEEN LEADING TO SETTLEMENT.

text.p: Intel Corp's counterclaim against Digital Equipment Corp gives the microprocessor manufacturer leverage and is likely to lead to an out-of-court settlement, analysts said.

In the latest volley in a legal row over patented technologies in U.S. District Court in Worcester, Mass. Intel's countersuit against Digital is claiming violation of 14 Intel patents. Depending upon the merits of Intel's claim, it will likely pressure Digital to negotiate a settlement, analysts said.
"I think this enhances the likelihood of a negotiated settlement. I think Intel wanted a little leverage here," said William Milton, an analyst with Brown Brothers Harriman.
The patent squabble has had little impact on business for the two companies thus far, but could become a major hindrance if a full-blown court battle ensued, analysts said.
"Court battles are expensive; the outcome is often unpredictable. They are time consuming. Even if one side wins, the case can be appealed," Milton added.
In May, Digital surprised the industry by filing suit against Intel, claiming it had stolen key elements of patented technology for the design of Intel's popular Pentium processors.

Intel's countersuit claims that Digital infringed patents covering microprocessor architecture and design, semiconductor manufacturing, video encoding/decoding, thermal management for portable systems, system architecture and design, and system service and management.
"Whether Intel is firing blanks or nuclear warheads remains to be seen," said Terry Shannon, editor of the independent newsletter "Shannon Knows DEC".
"Now, of course, that Intel has returned the favor to Digital, I think that makes it more likely that's there's going to be some sort of settlement," Shannon said.
Intel and Digital have reportedly held talks, but an Intel spokesman declined to comment if the two companies have held any recent negotiations.
"These are not frivolous patents," Intel spokesman Chuck Mulloy said. Nevertheless, he said the counterclaim was necessary only because Digital sued Intel.
"From a legal standpoint, we needed to maintain a more level playing field," Mulloy said. "That is the intent here, to defend ourselves. this is a defensive posture."
Digital did not immediately return phone calls seeking comment.

Charles Rule, an antitrust lawyer and former head of the antitrust division at the Department of Justice, said civil suits most often end in settlements. Patent suits are sometimes settled through cross-licensing deals with limited royalty agreements, he said.

"It's not unusual to see those kind of counterclaims filed," he said. "It is somewhat rare, although patents are somewhat different, that you litigate civil claims. So, it would not be surprising if they resolved them here."
Mulloy said Intel will ask the Worcester court to include its counterclaim in the lawsuit that Digital filed.
